results.name: trial_index_rating_correlation
results.description: Pearson correlation between trial_index and rating across all trials; observed more negative than null means people say yes less often as the session goes on, beyond what the stimulus order implies, and the model has no such drift.

results.name: mixed_cell_fraction
results.description: Fraction of (number_set, target) cells whose repeated answers are not unanimous (some yes and some no); observed above null means the model's p_yes is too extreme (people are less all-or-none than the near-hard commitment predicts), and below null means it is too graded.

results.name: single_example_generalization_rate
results.description: Yes rate on non-example targets for sets with exactly one example; observed above null means the model generalizes too narrowly from a single number (the size principle and commitment are too strong at n=1), and below null means it generalizes too broadly.
results.code:
# name: single_example_generalization_rate
# description: Yes rate on non-example targets for sets with exactly one example; observed above null means the model generalizes too narrowly from a single number (the size principle and commitment are too strong at n=1), and below null means it generalizes too broadly.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    mind = ex.sub(t, axis=0).abs().min(axis=1)
    n = ex.notna().sum(axis=1)
    m = ((n == 1) & (mind > 0)).values
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

results.name: yes_rate_target_is_example
results.description: Yes rate on trials where the target is itself one of the shown examples; observed below null means the model (near-zero lapse, all-or-none commitment) over-predicts endorsing the examples themselves (people say no to ~17% of them).
results.code:
# name: yes_rate_target_is_example
# description: Yes rate on trials where the target is itself one of the shown examples; observed below null means the model (near-zero lapse, all-or-none commitment) over-predicts endorsing the examples themselves (people say no to ~17% of them).
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    mind = ex.sub(t, axis=0).abs().min(axis=1)
    m = (mind == 0).values
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

results.name: square_set_square_target_lift
results.description: For sets of two or more examples that are all perfect squares, yes rate on non-example square targets minus yes rate on non-square targets; observed above null means the model's extra squares cost suppresses the 'perfect squares' reading more than people do, and below null means squares are even less available than modelled.
results.code:
# name: square_set_square_target_lift
# description: For sets of two or more examples that are all perfect squares, yes rate on non-example square targets minus yes rate on non-square targets; observed above null means the model's extra squares cost suppresses the 'perfect squares' reading more than people do, and below null means squares are even less available than modelled.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    mind = ex.sub(t, axis=0).abs().min(axis=1)
    n = ex.notna().sum(axis=1)
    S = [k * k for k in range(1, 11)]
    allsq = (ex.isin(S) | ex.isna()).all(axis=1) & (n >= 2)
    sq = t.isin(S)
    a = (allsq & sq & (mind > 0)).values
    b = (allsq & ~sq).values
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: inside_range_minus_near_outside
results.description: For multi-example sets, yes rate on non-example targets strictly between the smallest and largest example, minus yes rate on targets within 10 outside that span; observed above null means people fill in the examples' span more sharply than the model's intervals predict (the model extrapolates too much), and below null means the model fills in too much.
results.code:
# name: inside_range_minus_near_outside
# description: For multi-example sets, yes rate on non-example targets strictly between the smallest and largest example, minus yes rate on targets within 10 outside that span; observed above null means people fill in the examples' span more sharply than the model's intervals predict (the model extrapolates too much), and below null means the model fills in too much.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    mind = ex.sub(t, axis=0).abs().min(axis=1)
    n = ex.notna().sum(axis=1)
    lo = ex.min(axis=1)
    hi = ex.max(axis=1)
    inside = ((t > lo) & (t < hi) & (mind > 0) & (n > 1)).values
    outside = (((t < lo) | (t > hi)) & (mind <= 10) & (n > 1)).values
    if inside.sum() == 0 or outside.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[inside].mean() - r[outside].mean())

results.name: far_unrelated_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on targets more than 15 from every example, sharing no last digit with any example, and of the opposite parity to an all-even or all-odd set; observed above null means the model under-produces 'scattered guess' yeses to unrelated numbers (its baseline is too low), and below null means it over-produces them.
results.code:
# name: far_unrelated_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate on targets more than 15 from every example, sharing no last digit with any example, and of the opposite parity to an all-even or all-odd set; observed above null means the model under-produces 'scattered guess' yeses to unrelated numbers (its baseline is too low), and below null means it over-produces them.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    mind = ex.sub(t, axis=0).abs().min(axis=1)
    par = ex % 2
    alleven = (par.fillna(0) == 0).all(axis=1)
    allodd = (par.fillna(1) == 1).all(axis=1)
    mism = (alleven & (t % 2 == 1)) | (allodd & (t % 2 == 0))
    samel = (ex % 10).eq(t % 10, axis=0).any(axis=1)
    m = ((mind > 15) & ~samel & mism).values
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

results.name: parity_match_effect
results.description: For sets whose examples are all even or all odd, yes rate on non-example targets of the same parity minus yes rate on targets of the opposite parity; observed below null means the model over-uses odd/even concepts (it predicts too much parity-driven generalization), and above null means it under-uses them.
results.code:
# name: parity_match_effect
# description: For sets whose examples are all even or all odd, yes rate on non-example targets of the same parity minus yes rate on targets of the opposite parity; observed below null means the model over-uses odd/even concepts (it predicts too much parity-driven generalization), and above null means it under-uses them.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float)
    mind = ex.sub(t, axis=0).abs().min(axis=1)
    par = ex % 2
    alleven = (par.fillna(0) == 0).all(axis=1)
    allodd = (par.fillna(1) == 1).all(axis=1)
    same = ((alleven & (t % 2 == 0)) | (allodd & (t % 2 == 1))) & (mind > 0)
    opp = (alleven & (t % 2 == 1)) | (allodd & (t % 2 == 0))
    same, opp = same.values, opp.values
    if same.sum() == 0 or opp.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[same].mean() - r[opp].mean())
